data.source_title: Patterns of Communication through Interpreters: A Detailed Sociolinguistic Analysis
data.locator: Abstract; Methods; Results; Questions Asked by Patients (especially reported counts at lines 270-275 in rendered full text)
data.source_setting: Primary-care physicians with high-volume Hispanic practices in New York, California, Texas, and Florida; dyslipidemia visits
data.source_period: First published May 31, 2006; collection dates not stated in article text inspected
data.source_n: 16 patients with 9 physicians; 13 interpreted Spanish-English encounters and 3 Spanish encounters with one bilingual physician
data.unit: reported count of patient questions answered directly by interpreter and not conveyed to physician; the paper also reports 28 direct questions across 13 interpreted visits
data.source_evidence_basis: Audio/video-recorded visits were transcribed and analyzed using sociolinguistic/discourse methods. In the Questions Asked by Patients section, authors report 28 direct patient questions across 13 interpreted visits and 8 answered directly by interpreter without translation to physician. The same passage reports a mean of 1.75 questions per visit, which is internally inconsistent with 28/13 (approximately 2.15). These counts are retained with the discrepancy flagged; no mean is used. Authors also report reduced/revised speech and little rapport-building small talk in interpreted visits.
data.limitations: Small, selected primary-care sample involving Spanish-speaking patients discussing dyslipidemia; interpreters in all interpreted examples were family members (n=2) or nursing/office staff (n=11), not a representative sample of professional interpreters. The reported question count and mean are internally inconsistent. Cannot infer ED rates, language-general behavior, current practice, or local interpreter conduct.
data.inferred_scenario_use: Optional synthetic variation: patient asks a question through an interpreter; learner directs communication to the patient and ensures the question and response are conveyed through the interpreter. Do not depict the pattern as characteristic of any real interpreter or hospital.
